title: How to Read This Graph
oneLineScope: How this graph is organized, the edge-type legend, and where to start.
prose:
What this is. This tutorial covers the transformer and how the first large language models were trained — from the Attention Is All You Need paper (Vaswani et al., 2017) through the GPT and BERT families, the scaling-law results of Kaplan et al. (2020), and a brief terminal bridge to supervised fine-tuning and the earliest instruction-following models. It is not a survey of frontier systems, not a review of five years of architecture variations, and not a catalogue of every model released since 2020. The scope is a specific, bounded period, covered in depth: the ideas that made the transformer work and the results that revealed what scale could do.

The bargain. Twenty nodes, each long enough to give you the intuition and the mathematics to make the connections yourself. Every node is tethered to primary sources — the actual papers, pointed to by section number — and expository sources chosen for teaching quality. The goal is that when you finish a node you could explain the idea to a colleague and trust what you carry forward. Subtly wrong mental models are worse than ignorance; everything here is written to be trustworthy, and the annotations tell you exactly where to go when you want to verify.

Who this is for. A reader with strong mathematics and statistics, fluency in 1980s–1990s-era machine learning (connectionism, HMMs, statistical alignment, backpropagation), and no exposure to the post-2017 transformer literature. The tutorial treats linear algebra, probability, and optimization as native. It defines every term of art — token, embedding, attention head, logits, causal mask — on first use, in your vocabulary, and then uses it freely. Analogies from distributional semantics, statistical alignment, and connectionism are load-bearing, not decoration.

A graph, not a book

The material is organized as a directed graph, not a linear sequence of chapters. That reflects how the ideas actually hang together: some nodes are strict prerequisites for others; some stand as siblings that reward direct comparison; some exist mainly to set up what follows. A linear reading would bury the contrasts and conceal the real architecture of the field. The map below lets you navigate by interest and follow threads rather than march through a table of contents.

There are three kinds of edge, drawn distinctly in the map:

  • Prerequisite (solid arrow): understand the source node before the target. These form the backbone of the material. If a node’s explanation assumes a concept, that concept is a prerequisite.
  • Leads-to (warm-orange arrow): the source sets up the target as the natural next topic in the narrative arc, but the connection is motivational rather than strictly logical. You can enter the target independently; the source enriches it.
  • Contrast (dashed line, undirected): the two nodes are conceptual siblings worth examining side by side. The encoder–decoder fork in this graph — autoregressive LM, masked LM, and the encoder–decoder contrast node — is the main cluster of contrast edges.

Two entry points

The graph has two recommended starting points, both marked on the map.

Distributional semantics (node 02) is the on-ramp for the conceptually minded — for anyone coming from the Firth–Harris tradition of meaning-from-context that underpins corpus linguistics and early computational semantics. If the idea that a word’s meaning can be recovered from its distributional environment is native to you, this node bridges directly from that intuition to the dense learned representations that power the transformer. From there: distributional semantics leads to word embeddings, which is a prerequisite for scaled dot-product attention — and you are at the heart of the architecture.

Scaled dot-product attention (node 06) is the entry point for the impatient — for anyone who wants the core mechanism first and the conceptual prehistory afterward. Attention is the operation the entire transformer is built around; every other architectural choice is, at bottom, infrastructure for running attention at scale. If you know what soft, learned alignment looks like from statistical machine translation — IBM models, HMM-based alignment — you already have most of the intuition, and this node will feel like coming home.

Neither path is mandatory. Follow prerequisite edges when the dependencies matter; follow leads-to edges when you want the narrative thread; hop contrast edges when you want to compare siblings directly. The map is there to be used.

The shape of the journey

Five phases, moving left to right across the graph:

  1. Prehistory & foundations — the distributional and connectionist ideas the transformer draws on, the recurrent models it replaced, and the soft-alignment work in neural machine translation that directly anticipated attention.
  2. Core architecture — the scaled dot-product operation itself, multi-head attention, and positional encoding. This is the densest phase; almost everything else is built on it.
  3. The encoder–decoder fork — the residual-and-norm transformer block and the full encoder–decoder stack as published by Vaswani et al., then the fork into decoder-only (GPT lineage) and encoder-only (BERT) variants, with a contrast node to examine the tradeoffs directly.
  4. Training mechanics — tokenization and subword vocabularies, pretraining objectives, and optimization at scale: the choices that turn an architecture into a trained model.
  5. Scaling & the bridge — data and compute, scaling laws as a quantitative framework for predicting what more will buy you, in-context learning as a behavior that emerges at scale, and a brief terminal node on supervised fine-tuning and the step toward instruction-following models.

The bibliography

Every node carries a short annotated bibliography in two tiers. Primary sources are the original papers — the authority for exact claims; the annotations point you to the specific section or equation that matters. Exposition sources are secondary texts chosen for teaching quality, not citation count: Alammar’s Illustrated Transformer, the Annotated Transformer, Karpathy’s Zero to Hero, and the Jurafsky–Martin chapters appear throughout. The goal is that you are never more than one click from a source you can trust.

bibliography.citation: Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The anchor paper for this entire tutorial. §1 motivates the architecture; §3 defines scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and positional encoding; §5 gives the training recipe. Return to it often — it is short, dense, and precise.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. (3rd ed., draft). Speech and Language Processing. Chapters 6–11.
bibliography.annotation: The standard graduate-level NLP textbook, freely available. Chapters 6–7 cover vector semantics and embeddings (bridging from distributional semantics); chapters 9–11 cover RNNs, attention, and transformers with careful notation. Good companion for any node in the prehistory and architecture phases.
